AGAR: A REINFORCEMENT LEARNING SUBSTRATE
FOR LLM PROGRAM EVOLUTION
Haoran Li1, Zengle Ge2, Xiaomin Yuan2, YUI LO2, Haoxin Li3, Songlin Zhou3, Qianhui
Liu4,
Jiahua Ying2, Yuanhang Liu3, Mingju Chen5, Annan Li2, Jianmin Wu2, Dawei Yin2, Dou
Shen2
1University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
2Baidu
3Tsinghua University
4Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
5Shanghai University
ABSTRACT
Given a task and an evaluator, a language model can rewrite a candidate program
while a search loop decides which rewrites survive — a practical route to algo-
rithm discovery. But that loop is governed by five constants set by hand — which
parent to select, how hard to mutate, how to keep diversity, what to remember,
and a scalar score that never says which part of the program earned it — and rein-
forcement learning already has an estimator for each. The obstacle is that program
evolution is not usually written down as a decision process. We formalize it as a
Markov decision process whose action is the modular prefix the model is condi-
tioned on, not the program it emits, so that credit assignment, value estimation,
adaptive exploration and experience memory each attach to a distinct component.
AGAR (Algorithm Generation As RL) provides the substrate this licenses: any
estimator can be replaced or switched off without touching the controller, making
the transfer auditable one mechanism at a time, with no gradient training of the
backend model. Across 19 tasks, two backends and three seeds under one harness,
AGAR improves on the stronger of two published baselines on most tasks, with
the gains concentrated on the competitive-programming family. The formalization
also yields a checkable reading of prior work: these systems are implicitly zero-
discount, not by choice but because fitness is exogenous to an individual rather
than a return over successors, leaving a discount factor nothing to act on.
1
INTRODUCTION
A long-horizon algorithm optimization task — find a program that scores well on a task-specific
evaluator, given a budget of iterations and no gradient of the score with respect to the program text
— is a sequential decision problem. It is usually not written down as one. It is written down as an
evolutionary loop: maintain a population of programs, ask a language model to mutate or recombine
them, evaluate the offspring, keep what scores well, repeat (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov
et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025; Sharma, 2025). The results are real: improved bounds on open
combinatorial problems, faster kernels, better heuristics.
The thesis.
We take the position that such a task can be modelled as an RL problem, and that doing
so is not a re-labelling exercise: the modelling choices determine which machinery is applicable,
and the machinery then determines the system. Concretely, we formalize the loop as an MDP whose
action is the modular prefix the model is conditioned on — not the program it emits — and we
show that under that choice each load-bearing idea of modern RL (Sutton & Barto, 2018) attaches
to a distinct component of the loop. M1 (credit assignment), M2 (value estimation), M3 (adaptive
exploration) and M4 (experience memory) are the places the modelling says the estimators go. We
are deliberate about the strength of that claim: the formalization forces which kinds of estimator
the objective requires and whether each is an action factor or retrieved context, but it does not
force that there are four of them, and the boundaries we draw between M1, M2 and M3 are a
factorization we chose rather than one the mathematics uniquely picks out. What we contribute is
a general evolutionary substrate that carries this decomposition: an interface in which any one of
1
arXiv:2610.09215v1  [cs.AI]  6 Oct 2026


--- Page 2 ---
the estimators can be replaced or switched off without touching the controller, so that the transfer is
auditable one mechanism at a time.
The gap and the obstacle.
What the LLM contributes today is the mutation operator. Everything
that decides where to mutate, how hard, and what to remember is a hand-set constant: five decisions,
each with an estimator RL already has. The obstacle is not reward density — RL routinely operates
under terminal-only reward, and LLM-driven program evolution does receive intermediate signal
which the mutation operator consumes. The real difference is structural. In RL the value of a state
is defined recursively over its successors, so terminal credit is propagable in principle. In evolution,
fitness is an exogenous property of an individual; no Bellman equation relates a parent’s fitness
to its children’s, so there is no recursion to propagate along at all. We make this precise in §2.1.
The formalization below makes the recursion definable over the search without claiming to make
the backup empirical: the value it recurses on is estimated in text space rather than learned from
observed returns, and that boundary stays exactly where it is.
A checkable reading of prior work.
Because the action is a prefix conditioning a frozen black-
box model, the objective is J(π) = E[P
t γtrt] + λH(π). Setting γ=0 recovers the selection rule
every system in this literature uses (Observation 1): immediate fitness plus a population entropy
term. This is not a metaphor but a degeneracy — and not a criticism, since without a recursion a
discount factor has nothing to act on. Making the recursion definable is what turns γ into a tunable
knob.
A substrate, not a system.
The substrate (§5) carries the transfer: interchangeable modules, in-
terchangeable execution backends, native asynchrony. Its engineering problems are those of asyn-
chronous RL post-training stacks (Luo et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; miles Contributors, 2025; Hou
et al., 2026); the optimand differs (text, not weights) and there is no gradient.
Contributions.
1. A modelling of algorithm optimization as RL and the substrate it licenses (§3). Action-
as-prefix makes five RL tools expressible in text space, each replacing a named fixed rule in a
specific module. The γ=0 degeneracy falls out of the same formalization. The contribution is an
interface auditable one mechanism at a time, not a uniqueness result.
2. Modular TextGrad: policy improvement in text space (§4). Each module’s persistent guide-
lines — the text-space analogue of policy weights — are optimized without gradient training.
We report a measurement of the operator: a local-edit and validation-revert design that replaces
the original rewrite operator (§4.2).
3. Asynchronous execution and the credit-assignment problem it creates (§5.2, §5.3). The
streaming scheduler creates staleness: credit is assigned against a population that no longer
exists. We characterize τ empirically (naive τ ≤W−1 is refuted in practice) and relate it to
asynchronous RL post-training (Hou et al., 2026).
2
BACKGROUND: TWO INDEPENDENT LINEAGES
Evolutionary computation searches by maintaining a population, perturbing it, and keeping what
scores well. Genetic programming applied this to program spaces decades ago (Koza, 1992); the
LLM era replaced the syntax-tree mutation operator with a language model, which is what made
the approach competitive on real algorithm-design problems (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov
et al., 2025). Later systems differ in how they manage the population — ShinkaEvolve adds a
bandit over LLM backends and novelty sampling (Lange et al., 2025); SMC-based variants replace
generational selection with sequential Monte Carlo resampling (Jiang et al., 2026); EvoX makes the
search strategy itself the object of evolution (Liu et al., 2026) — but they share the structure of the
signal. Fitness attaches to a completed individual, not to a step of a trajectory, and intermediate
information informs the generation of the next candidate without ever accumulating into a return.
The search state — which lineages are productive, which regions are exhausted — is therefore
carried implicitly in the population rather than estimated.
2


--- Page 3 ---
Reinforcement learning developed a different toolkit because it assumed a different structure, a tra-
jectory over which value is recursively defined: credit assignment propagates outcome information
backwards along it (Sutton, 1988); value estimation predicts return before it is observed (Mnih
et al., 2015); adaptive exploration makes the explore/exploit trade-off a decision rather than a con-
stant (Auer et al., 2002; Garivier & Moulines, 2011); entropy regularization turns diversity into an
objective term (Haarnoja et al., 2018); and experience replay makes the run’s history a learnable
resource (Lin, 1992; Schaul et al., 2016). Our five transferred tools are these five, and §3.3 states
what each had to become.
2.1
WHAT ACTUALLY SEPARATES THEM
It is tempting to say that RL has dense reward, evolution has sparse reward, and that this is the
obstacle. That is inaccurate in both directions: RL routinely operates under terminal-only reward,
and LLM-driven program evolution does receive intermediate signal which the mutation operator
consumes. The real difference is structural. In RL, the value of a state is defined recursively in terms
of its successors, and terminal credit is in principle propagable along that recursion via returns or
TD(λ) — sparse reward makes this statistically hard, but the problem stays well-posed. In evolution,
fitness is an exogenous property of an individual; a child is not a successor state reached by acting
in the parent’s state but a new object emitted by a stochastic operator, and no Bellman equation
relates a parent’s fitness to its children’s. There is therefore nothing to back up along, which is why
evolutionary search assigns credit by survival rather than by attribution.
The formalization of §3 supplies the missing structure: by defining the action as a prefix and the
transition as one generation step, it makes a Bellman recursion well-posed over the search. It does
not supply the missing signal: our VM2 is an estimate produced by a text-space heuristic, not a value
learned by backing up observed returns. What is live is the forward half — the estimate computed at
dispatch — through two channels active in every reported run: the M3 selection rule f(p) + γV (p)
and the M2 lineage ranking. So:
We make the recursion definable. We do not make the backup empirical.
This also explains Observation 1: prior systems are γ=0 not because their designers chose greedi-
ness, but because without a recursion a discount factor has no successor value to act on.
2.2
POSITIONING
The recurring distinction between AGAR and the closest prior systems is that a rule which is fixed
elsewhere becomes a learnable, replaceable component here (Appendix D.6 gives a row-by-row
comparison). A parallel line of work builds substrates for applying RL to agents at scale (Luo
et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; miles Contributors, 2025), together with asynchronous post-training
systems such as SAO (Hou et al., 2026). These are our closest methodological relatives: they share
our engineering problems — decompose the loop into independently swappable components, make
rollouts asynchronous, bound the staleness that asynchrony introduces — but in every one of them
the learnable object is a set of model weights updated by a policy-gradient estimator, whereas here
the model is frozen and the learnable object is the text that conditions it.
3
FORMALIZATION AND THE TRANSFER
3.1
LLM-DRIVEN PROGRAM EVOLUTION AS AN MDP
We model one evolutionary step as a transition in an MDP (S, A, P, R, γ). Figure 1 shows the whole
construction at once; the subsections below take its parts in turn.
State st is mixed-granularity by necessity: an individual-level part (the parent program, its fitness,
its lineage, its age, its mutation history) and a population-level part (fitness statistics, a diversity
measure, budget progress and remainder). Both are required — credit assignment and value esti-
mation are questions about an individual, exploration and entropy about a population — and neither
subsumes the other: a purely individual state cannot express “the population has converged”, and a
purely population-level state cannot express “this lineage has stalled”.
3


--- Page 4 ---
Figure 1: The transfer as a whole. Left to right: the mixed-granularity state st; the policy π, whose
action at is the modular text prefix M1–M3 produce, with M4 supplying retrieved context rather
than an action factor; the environment, in which the frozen black-box LLM sees only that prefix
plus the task description and parent code, and a pluggable selection operator folds the result back
into the population; and the reward terms of Eq. equation 2. The outer arrows are the two loops that
make this RL rather than a re-labelling: the TextGrad update over the module guidelines θi (top),
and the st →st+1 transition the search itself performs (bottom).
Action at is a modular prefix, not a program. This is the load-bearing choice of the formalization.
It is tempting to call the generated program the action, but the program is sampled from a frozen
black-box LLM: it is a product of the transition, not something the search policy emits. What the

rather than relabel: π is a text-emitting object improvable without touching model weights (§4), and
the module boundary is fixed by which factor of at a component writes rather than by taste.
Transition P has three stages: the execution LLM samples a program conditioned on at and the
parent; an evaluator returns a scalar fitness; a selection operator folds the offspring into the popula-
tion. The first stage is a frozen black box with no accessible likelihood, which forces a model-free
treatment. The third is pluggable, which is where value-guided selection enters (Table 5).

of the horizon parameter that controls how much lineage the modules see (see Appendix D.2 for
defaults).
3.2
THE OBJECTIVE, AND THE γ=0 DEGENERACY

(3)
We instantiate H(π) as mean pairwise code distance within the population, with a behaviour-class
Shannon entropy as a secondary indicator. The choice is deliberate: it costs zero additional LLM
calls and is already monitored by M3, so the entropy term is measurable at every step rather than
estimated. We add no KL penalty; unlike RLHF there is no natural reference policy to stay close to.
Observation 1 (Existing systems are the γ=0 special case) Setting γ=0 in Eq. equation 2 deletes
the VM2 term and collapses Eq. equation 3 to E[r0] + λH(π), i.e. a one-step objective in which an
individual is worth exactly its immediate fitness improvement plus its contribution to population
statistics. This is precisely the selection rule used by every LLM program-evolution system we are
aware of.
Observation 1 is an algebraic identity, not a metaphor, and it is the cleanest reading the formalization
gives us of the prior art: γ is a knob whose zero setting reproduces a one-step objective, because a
discount factor with no successor value to act on has nothing else to be. We state it as an identity
over Eq. equation 2 and leave the empirical consequences of setting γ > 0 to future work.
We read this as a consequence of §2.1 rather than a shortcoming of prior work. A discount factor
needs a successor value; absent a recursion over the search there is none, so γ=0 is the only setting
available. What §3.1 contributes is not a better choice of γ but the structure that gives γ a referent
at all — with the honest counterpart that the VM2 it multiplies is estimated in text space rather than
bootstrapped from observed returns.
3.3
THE TRANSFER
Table 5 in Appendix D.7 is the centre of the paper. Each row names an RL tool, the evolutionary
fixed rule it displaces, the module it becomes, and — most importantly — what had to change given
the absence of an empirical backup (§2.1).
We stress the direction of derivation. We did not choose four modules and then find RL names for
them; the four factors of at in Eq. equation 1 plus the retrieved context M4 are what the transfer
produces, and the fact that M4 is not a factor of the action — it is context — is a consequence of the
formalization rather than an implementation detail.
5


--- Page 6 ---
Instantiations.
A choice of implementation for each of M1–M4 defines a point in a configuration
space (§5.1). Throughout the paper we report two such points, Base and Combo, differing in the
M2 estimator and the M3 decision rule (statistical vs. LLM-based; rule-based vs. discounted-UCB).
They are sampled points, not competing systems; we do not argue for one over the other.
3.4
CRITIC INDEPENDENCE, AND WHAT IT FORCES
Each module is improved against its own critic, which judges only whether that module’s output
was correct on its own terms — was the attribution consistent with the observed lineage? did the
predicted ranking match the realized ordering? — and never attempts to apportion final fitness
across modules. The reason is structural: all four outputs are concatenated into one prefix (Eq. 1)
and consumed jointly by a black-box LLM, so their contributions to the resulting program are not
separable from the inside. This has a design consequence: which transferred tool carries the gain can
only be answered by external leave-one-out ablation, not from inside the system. We do not report
that decomposition: at n=3 the level-to-level differences of Table 2 already sit inside the noise. See
Appendix D.1 for the full module data contracts.
4
MODULAR TEXTGRAD: POLICY IMPROVEMENT IN TEXT SPACE
Section 3 defines what we optimize. This section defines how: the method is TextGrad (Yuksekgonul
et al., 2024) applied to a target its original formulation already fits — an objective with no analytic
gradient, computed by an external system, over a variable that is itself text. The frozen backend
model writes code; each module’s persistent guidelines θi are the variable being optimized; the loss
is ˆr of §3; and the “gradient” is the rollout context shown to the LLM critic. Appendix D.5 gives the
full operator definitions and the RL-to-text correspondence table.
Two features of our instance are unlike the tasks TextGrad was demonstrated on. First, the variable
is modular: the policy is a concatenation of per-module guidelines, so the gradient must be taken per
module and a critique that conflates them is unusable. Second, the loss is measured over a period
of noisy evolutionary steps rather than a single forward pass, so the update rests on a small-sample
signal and must decide what to do when that signal is inconclusive. The second feature is what §4.2
is about.
4.1
OPERATORS
For each module i we define a per-module textual gradient operator Gi and a shared update operator
U (full definitions in Appendix D.5). The object θi is the module’s persistent guidelines: a block
of text that survives across evolutionary steps and conditions every subsequent invocation of that
module — not the module’s per-step output, which is an action, not a policy parameter. Optimiz-
ing the output instead of the guidelines would fail to persist and therefore cannot constitute policy
improvement.
4.2
WHAT WE MEASURED, AND WHY THE OPERATOR WAS REPLACED
The rewrite operator — critique in, new guidelines out, unconditionally — is the direct transposition
of TextGrad to this setting. Two measurements over 206 runs (9,844 update pairs) forced its replace-
ment. (i) The variable was resampled, not improved: the guideline block hit its 2000-character
budget at the first update of every run and stayed there; textual similarity between adjacent versions
was 0.18, between first and last 2–6%, without exception. (ii) Nothing closed the loop: a rewrite
that made things worse persisted until the next rewrite replaced it, so there is no mechanism by
which θi at step 100 should beat θi at step 1.
The repaired operator replaces U with a local edit plus deferred validation. The policy is an ex-
plicit numbered rule list; Gi returns at most one ADD and one EDIT/REMOVE per period (NONE
is an expected answer); validation is deferred verdict lag periods because a new rule’s children
are mostly leaves at install time, making immediate scoring equivalent to γ=0. Cost falls from 8
to 2 LLM calls per update (only M1 and M4 are edited; the other two were writing guidelines no
code path read). The budget is bounded by construction, and the operator became legible: discrete
6


--- Page 7 ---
rules with provenance can be reported at run end, which the rewrite operator made impossible. Full
measurement detail is in Appendix D.5.
5
SUBSTRATE: EXTENSIBILITY AND ASYNCHRONOUS EXECUTION
A modelling choice only becomes a system if the interfaces it implies are real. This section describes
the two properties of the substrate the transfer actually depends on — replaceable components and
native asynchrony — and one problem the second creates for the first. We develop the asynchronous
part against the closest engineering precedent, the asynchronous RL post-training systems surveyed
in §2.
5.1
EXTENSIBILITY, STATED SO THAT IT CAN BE CHECKED
“Extensible” is easy to assert, and every substrate paper asserts it. We give three measurable forms.
(a) Configuration space: the choice of implementation for M1 × M2 × M3 × M4 spans 180 con-
figurations, of which we have evaluated 14; Base and Combo are two of those points. (b) Inte-
gration cost: replacing M3’s LLM explore/exploit call with the discounted-UCB bandit of Garivier
& Moulines (2011) added 236 lines in one new module file and changed 0 lines in the controller
or the module protocol — and deleted 26 lines of hand-written budget and stagnation heuristic that
the discounting subsumes. That deletion is the part we would point to: the claim is not that new
mechanisms are cheap to add, but that adding a principled one can remove a hand-tuned constant.
(c) Interchangeable backends, and a non-obvious cost. Backends register through a single entry
point and can be swapped between a thread pool and a distributed runtime. During development
this produced a failure worth reporting: under the distributed backend, per-task serialization gives
each rollout an isolated module instance for free, while under the thread-pool backend a shared
evaluator instance guarded by an environment lock caused rollouts to be silently serialized — no
error, no warning, and worse the longer each evaluation takes, i.e. exactly on the workloads where
concurrency matters most. The fix was explicit per-task isolation of module state. The general
lesson is that extensibility is not freedom; it is an obligation on the interface to state its isolation
semantics. An interface permitting a backend swap without specifying whether state is shared has
not made the system extensible, only replaceable. Appendix D.9 gives the integration diff in full.
5.2
ASYNCHRONOUS EXECUTION
The scheduler is streaming rather than generational: it fills W in-flight rollouts, waits for the first
to complete, folds the result into the population, and immediately dispatches a replacement. There
is no batch barrier, so a single slow evaluation delays one slot rather than the whole generation —
which matters here because per-rollout times across the tasks we study span 3.7× (median 269 s
on the fastest task against 1007 s on the slowest), so a straggler holds a slot for several times the
median. As an engineering decision this needs no justification: it is what every production RL stack
does, and the reasons are the same.
The interesting part is what the asynchrony does to the learning rule, and it is here that the evolu-
tionary setting diverges from the RL one.
Comparison with asynchronous RL post-training.
The asynchrony forces single-rollout con-
sumption, which is the native form for evolutionary rollouts (each offspring is scored against the
population, not against siblings) rather than a concession. SAO (Hou et al., 2026) reaches the same
design from the post-training side; Appendix D.9 details the two further points of contact that look
like correspondences but are not.
5.3
STALENESS: WHAT ASYNCHRONY DOES TO CREDIT ASSIGNMENT
The dispatch path samples a parent, computes the M2 estimate, and runs the M3 decision at dispatch
time; the resulting fitness lands some number of population updates later. Call that gap τ, so τ ≡0
is the synchronous case. τ has no a priori upper bound: because the scheduler is streaming, a
slow rollout can outlive an arbitrary number of faster ones, and τ is bounded only by the tail of the
7


--- Page 8 ---
Figure 2: The substrate. Top: the streaming loop — fill W slots, wait for any completion, dispatch a
replacement immediately — with the controller as sole writer of the population and the W in-flight
rollouts reading a dispatch-time snapshot and writing only their own trajectory. The four pipeline
stages (SELECT, GENERATE, EVALUATE, JUDGE) are the substrate’s; the replaceable modules sit in
the SELECT slot. Shared resource pools are acquired per use and returned. Bottom: the same loop in
the three moments used throughout this paper, with τ defined as the population-version difference
between dispatch and landing.
evaluation-time distribution. Bounding it at W−1 would require the generational synchronisation
we rejected for throughput. We therefore characterise τ empirically rather than bounding it; the
measured distribution is in Appendix D.4, where at W=8 the maximum is 22 against a naive bound
of 7.

The consequence connects to Table 5: credit is assigned against a population that no longer exists.
M2’s baseline statistics are τ updates old; M3’s selection rule consumes a value estimate computed
against a superseded population; M4’s novelty distances are computed against a stale population;
and the Meta layer consumes a rollout buffer produced under superseded guidelines — which is
precisely the sense in which §4’s operator is off-policy. The standard correction does not transfer:
SAO’s clipped importance ratio needs the two policies to be comparable per token, and our “policy”
is a block of natural language that an update may replace wholesale. A clipping-style correction
would require first defining a distance between two texts and arguing that it bounds a likelihood
ratio, and we have no such argument. We report the delay instead of correcting it.
6
EXPERIMENTS
We ask two questions, both of which the formalization makes answerable: (i) does the transfer help
at all, under one harness and against published systems? (ii) how much of that is the accumulated
substrate? The third component of the paper’s evidence is Observation 1 itself, which is an algebraic
identity over Eq. equation 2 and therefore requires no experiment; we state it here as a fact about the
construction and leave the empirical consequences of the discount to future work.
6.1
SETUP
Tasks. 19 tasks in three families: 10 competitive-programming heuristic-optimization problems
(C++), 3 mathematical construction problems, and 6 systems/ML algorithm-discovery problems
(Python). Median per-rollout time differs across tasks by 3.7× (269–1007 s) and score scales differ
entirely, so all aggregation is on per-task normalized scores.
Models, seeds and baselines. 2 backend models (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2) × 3 seeds; we
treat n=3 as supporting qualitative conclusions only. Baselines are OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve,
run under their own harnesses with task specifications ported by us, plus vanilla — our substrate
with every transferred module disabled. vanilla is the scientifically important baseline; the external
systems are the comparability check.
6.2
QUALITY AT MATCHED BUDGET
Both instantiations of AGAR rank above both baselines on DeepSeek; Base leads on GLM with
Combo close behind. The standard deviation of AGAR is noticeably lower than that of the baselines,
partly because five tasks are near-ceiling for all systems (circle, cloudcast, erdos, first ac, prism):
on those tasks every normalized score is close to 1.0, which suppresses variance. The meaningful
signal is on the remaining 14 tasks, and the ALE (competitive programming) family carries most of
the gain.
6.3
DOES THE TRANSFER WORK, AND HOW MUCH IS THE SUBSTRATE?
The mechanisms this substrate carries fall into two groups that have to be ablated separately, be-
cause each group is held fixed inside the other group’s comparison. The substrate layers (L0–L3)
are active in both arms of any module ablation and so cancel in its difference; conversely the trans-
ferred modules are active at every substrate level. This section reports the substrate ladder, which
9


--- Page 10 ---
is the comparison we can make with complete data. The module-level decomposition is a separate
measurement, and §7 explains why we do not report it.
The substrate ladder, accumulated.
Each level adds exactly one thing to the one below it. L0
is repeated sampling — rewrite the current best and nothing else; L1 adds inspiration samples and
a natural-language critic, i.e. naive evolution; L2 adds a prioritized replay buffer (island pruning,
purge, diversity slots); and L3 adds sample-level credit assignment (a per-test-case weakness report).
L2 and L3 are exactly the Base and Combo of Table 1, so this ladder is also what separates those
two instantiations.

This ladder must be read carefully, and we read it narrowly. End-to-end (L0 →L3) the mean
gains +14.6%, and L0 is a genuine floor: it is the substrate running a bare rewrite loop with every
accumulated mechanism switched off. That is the comparison which shows the mechanisms are
doing work rather than the harness.
But per task the ladder is not monotone, and we do not claim that each added level helps. L1 →
L2 falls on three of five tasks and the overall mean dips slightly (0.8465 →0.8425); ahc015 declines
from L1 through L3 (0.9835 →0.8284) and ahc024 is flat. Two of the five tasks carry essentially
the whole mean gain (ahc008 +66.2%, ahc016 +52.7%). At n=3 the level-to-level differences sit
inside the noise, and the per-task non-monotonicity is the direct evidence of that. What the table
supports is that the accumulated stack is worth +14.6% over the bare loop — not an attribution of
that figure to any one level.
7
DISCUSSION
What the transfer does and does not establish.
The formalization of §3 buys three things: a
precise sense in which the prior art is a special case (Observation 1), a factorization of the loop into
modules that the objective constrains but does not uniquely determine, and a vocabulary in which
mechanisms from the RL literature can be stated, implemented and compared inside an evolutionary
loop. What it buys, in one sentence, is that the Bellman recursion becomes definable over evolu-
tionary search. What it does not buy is an empirical backup: the value the recursion consumes is
estimated in text space rather than learned from observed returns. The two data-backed limitations
and the full unverified list appear in Appendix D.8.
Future work.
The most direct next step is wiring the TD correction into the loop, turning M2 from
a one-shot estimator into a learned one. Beyond that: importance correction for staleness (Hou et al.,
2026); cross-model critics; leave-one-out module ablation at larger n; standardizing the V scale so
γ>0 can be tested cleanly; and using the 180-configuration space of §5.1 to ask which regions of
mechanism space are worth exploring — a question that only becomes askable once mechanisms
are interchangeable.

A
STATEMENT ON THE USE OF AI ASSISTANTS
LLMs were used in this work in two distinct roles, which we separate deliberately.
As the object of study.
The system described in this paper invokes large language models as its
mutation operator, as its module policies, and as the critics of §4. These uses are the subject matter
of the paper and are documented in §3–§5 and Appendix B, including model identifiers, decoding
parameters and call accounting.
As a writing and coding aid.
The authors used an LLM-based assistant for implementation
and analysis support: refactoring module code, writing the experiment submission and result-
aggregation scripts, computing the summary statistics reported in §6.3 from the raw run artifacts,
and revising LaTeX prose. It was also used to audit consistency between the manuscript and the
implementation, which is how several discrepancies between the two were located. All scientific
claims, experimental designs, analyses and conclusions are the authors’. The authors verified every
reported number against the raw experimental artifacts and take full responsibility for the content of
the paper, including any errors.
No AI system is listed as an author.
B
REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
§6.1 gives the task suite, the two backend models and the budget. Table 1 reports the normalised
mean across all 19 tasks per condition (each task score divided by the per-task maximum, then aver-
aged); per-task raw scores and the full two-backend detail are in Appendix D.10. Table 2 reports the
same for each substrate level. Seeds are fixed at 42, 123 and 456 throughout and control population
initialization and sampling order; every condition is three seeds × 100 fitness evaluations, with no
exceptions.
The metric is best-at-budget on each task’s own objective, normalized per task for aggregation only.
The saturation criterion — all four conditions within 1% — was applied before ranks were in-
spected, and the tasks it excludes are marked in Table 1. Decoding uses temperature 0.7 and a
393,216-token cap; top-p is left at the serving default rather than pinned, which we note because it
is part of the sampling distribution we do not control. Both backends are hosted models rather than
frozen artifacts, so exact reproduction of absolute scores may not be possible; we regard the relative
comparisons as the reproducible content.
§6.3 states which conclusions are limited by sample size: at n=3 the level-to-level differences of
the substrate ladder sit inside the noise, which is why we report the end-to-end figure and decline
to attribute it to any single level, and why no per-module leave-one-out decomposition is reported.
Baseline numbers are obtained by us running OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve under our own evalua-
tion protocol, with task specifications ported by us, rather than copied from the cited papers. Those
ports are part of the release, since the baseline conditions are other people’s systems and should be
independently auditable. Runs execute in a container image released with the code, each allocated
four CPU cores and 16 GiB of memory with no GPU; per-run LLM call counts and token counts are
12


--- Page 13 ---
logged. The framework, all module implementations, every task specification, the exact configura-
tion file for each reported run, and the raw logs will be released publicly upon publication. Each run
directory in the release contains the configuration actually used, so any reported cell traces to the
settings that produced it rather than to a described protocol.
C
ETHICS STATEMENT
This work studies automated algorithm discovery on benchmark optimization problems: no human
subjects, no personal data, no demographically sensitive attributes. Every generated program is
executed in a sandboxed evaluation environment and none is deployed. Compute expenditure is the
one cost we consider material, and we quantify it rather than elide it.
D
ADDITIONAL MATERIAL
D.1
MODULE INTERFACES
Each module is a class implementing the substrate’s Module protocol, invoked with two arguments:
a read-only context (the experiment-level world — population snapshot, configuration, accessors)
and a writable result (the per-rollout trajectory). That split is what makes the concurrency safe
(§5.2): a worker never writes the world, and the controller never reads a worker’s intermediate state.
The data contract below is taken from the implementations rather than paraphrased, because it is
what makes the module boundary checkable: a component’s identity is which field of at it writes.
Module
Reads
Writes
M1 credit
population accessor
m1 prefix (str)
rl evolve metadata
M2 value
population accessor
m2 ranking (list)
child stats
m2 v scores (dict)
lineage tree
m2 prefix (str)
M3 exploration
population accessor
result.selection
m2 ranking
m3 prefix (str)
m2 v scores
m3 decision (str)
M4 memory
rollout history
retrieved context for M1–M3
Two structural facts are visible in this table and are worth stating because they are the con-
tent of §3’s claim rather than implementation detail. First, M3 is the only module that writes
result.selection: it is the sole Actor, while M2 writes a ranking and never a decision. Sec-
ond, M4 writes no prefix field — it is retrieved context consumed by the other three, which is why
it carries no θi and is not a factor of the action.
The modules execute strictly in sequence, M1 →M2 →M3, then generation, evaluation and
judging. M3 depends on M2’s ranking; M1 and M2 are mutually independent and could in principle
run concurrently, but the implementation does not do this and we do not claim it.
D.2
REWARD AND ENTROPY DETAILS
Defaults for Eq. equation 2: γ = 0.95 (with γ = 0 as the degenerate arm of Observation 1),
wmax = 0.7, wmean = 0.3, λ = 0.1.
H(π) is instantiated as the mean pairwise cosine distance between the feature vectors of population
members, 1 −⟨vi, vj⟩/(∥vi∥∥vj∥), averaged over all pairs with both vectors present. Programs
without a feature vector are skipped rather than imputed. The quantity costs no additional LLM
calls and M3 already monitors it for its diversity floor, which is why the entropy term is measured
at every step rather than estimated.
We report no sensitivity sweep over λ. The weights above were fixed before the reported runs and
not tuned against them; given that n=3 leaves the level-to-level differences of Table 2 inside the
13


--- Page 14 ---
noise, a sweep at this sample size would not be able to separate λ settings either, and we prefer to
state that than to report a sweep that cannot resolve what it appears to measure.
D.3
TASK SUITE
Nineteen tasks in three families. The competitive-programming family is drawn from AtCoder
Heuristic Contest problems (ahc008–ahc046), scored by each contest’s own objective.
The
mathematical-construction family (erdos, first ac, second ac) scores a constructed object against
a target bound. The systems/ML family (circle, cloudcast, eplb, llm sql, prism, txn) scores a
discovered algorithm on a held-out workload.
Score scales are not comparable across tasks — prism reports values near 26, cloudcast near
0.0016, txn in the thousands — so every aggregate in this paper is computed on per-task normalized
scores and every table reports raw scores per task. Median per-rollout wall-clock time ranges from
269 s (eplb) to 1007 s (ahc016), a 3.7× spread; this is the straggler profile that motivates streaming
dispatch (§5.2).
Six tasks are classified saturated — circle, cloudcast, erdos, first ac, prism on both backends, plus
ahc026, which reaches the same ceiling by 200 evaluations. The criterion is that all four conditions
fall within 1%, and it was applied before ranks were inspected. The independent evidence that this
classification is not post-hoc is the behaviour of the substrate ladder, where the saturated tasks cluster
at a ceiling across every level.
D.4
STALENESS MEASUREMENTS
Table 3 gives the empirical distribution of τ under the W-sweep. τ is computed at landing time as
the population-version at landing minus the version stamped at dispatch. At W=1 the scheduler is
synchronous, so τ ≡0 strictly — this is a calibration check on the instrumentation itself; every row
with W>1 is therefore a measurement, not an accounting artefact.

Two patterns are worth noting. First, the mean tracks 0.88 (W−1) on both tasks across the full
sweep — well below the naive W−1 scaling but clearly non-zero, so staleness is real and cannot be
treated as negligible. Second, the tail is heavy and does not converge: at W=8 roughly one in five
rollouts exceeds W−1, and the maximum of 22 is more than three times the naive bound, a value
that would require generational synchronisation to suppress.
Completion detection is by insertion-order scan with a 5 s polling timeout, so rollouts finishing
inside the same poll window fold into the population in dispatch order rather than true completion
order. Against a median rollout time of several hundred seconds this biases the measured distribution
negligibly, but it is a measurement convention rather than an exact observable and we state it as such.
The originally planned second column — the relationship between τ and M2 estimation error — is
not reported. τ is written to the run log but is not threaded into M2’s statistics, so the per-rollout
correspondence between the two quantities is not available. Establishing it would require plumbing
the dispatch version number through to the value estimator, which we have not done.

D.7
THE TRANSFER
D.8
LIMITATIONS (FULL LIST)
• Per-module attribution is unresolved. The substrate ladder (Table 2) reports end-to-end gain
but no leave-one-out decomposition of the four transferred modules; which of M1–M4 carries
the gain is open.
• M2 is an estimator, not a value function. It is not trained against realized descendant fitness, so
the γVM2 term carries whatever bias the text-space heuristic has, with no mechanism to correct
it over the run.
• V ’s “orthogonality” is partly self-inflicted. V correlates negatively with fitness, which we
read as carrying information fitness cannot see; but V is also what selects parents, and those
descendants’ gains are what define V . The correlation is in part manufactured by the selection
rule itself.

• γ only discriminates among individuals with descendant evidence. lineage return car-
ries a horizon: programs born within the last horizon iterations score V =0 and the ranking
tie-breaks back to fitness, so γ’s discriminative power applies to older individuals.
• Unequal LLM budget. At matched evaluations we spend 2–4× the baselines’ calls; we report
no LLM-call-matched arm.
• TextGrad has no convergence guarantee, and its measured effect is confounded by the redun-
dant signal path identified in §4.
• M2 bootstrapping. The estimator calibrates itself with its own estimates; we observe no diver-
gence but offer no argument that it cannot occur.
• Critic and module share a backend model, so self-evaluation blind spots are possible; a cross-
model critic is left to future work.
• Scope. 3 seeds support qualitative conclusions only; 2 backend models; main runs are single-
worker.
• Baseline fairness. Baseline systems are ported by us; our ports are released so the conditions
can be checked independently.
D.9
EXTENSIBILITY CASE STUDY
The integration reported in §5.1(b) replaces M3’s LLM explore/exploit decision with the discounted-
UCB bandit of Garivier & Moulines (2011). The arms are EXPLOIT and EXPLORE; on each update
every arm’s discounted pull count and reward sum decay by a factor g before the played arm is
credited, and the decision is arg maxa sa/na + c
p
log(N+1)/na. Cold start plays the least-pulled
arm until both have at least one discounted pull.
The diff is 236 lines in one new module file. The new class subclasses the existing M3 and over-
rides parent selection; it preserves the output contract exactly (result.selection plus the
m3 prefix and m3 decision metadata of Appendix D.1). Neither the controller nor the mod-
ule protocol is modified: the substrate contains zero references to this mechanism, and it is selected
by one configuration key.
Integrating it also deleted 26 lines — the hand-written budget and stagnation decay heuristic that the
discounting subsumes. That deletion is the part we would point to: the claim of §5.1 is not that new
mechanisms are cheap to add, but that adding a principled one can remove a hand-tuned constant,
which is the same claim the paper makes about the transfer as a whole.
We note the limit of this case study honestly. The bandit is off by default and is not used in any
reported run (§7), so what this demonstrates is that the interface admits the mechanism at the stated
cost — not that the mechanism helps.
